Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The writer effectively uses exposition and summary at the beginning to establish the premise of Daniel's recurring dreams and provide background on his past marriage to Rachel and his current life with Isabel. Once this foundation is laid, the narrative smoothly transitions into dramatized, real-time scenes—such as the Sunday afternoon conversation while repotting a plant, the late-night confession in bed, the discovery of the keys, and the final canoeing trip. The writer weaves short bursts of summary between these scenes to compress time (e.g., summarizing how the dreams changed over weeks or compressing the history of his failed marriage into a paragraph) while relying on vivid dialogue and character interaction in the scenes to drive the emotional arc forward.
